newsitem.title: UK: Aberfan remembers generation wiped out in minutes.
newsitem.headline: Aberfan remembers generation wiped out in minutes.

text.p: The people of Aberfan, heads bowed in communal grief, paid tribute on Monday to a generation of children wiped out 30 years ago when a coal tip collapsed on the village school.

With morning mist barely risen from the valley, survivors and relatives gathered in the hillside cemetery of this tight-knit Welsh mining town to commemorate the 116 children and 28 adults killed in Britain's worst landslide disaster.
"What a terrible price to pay," said Cliff Minett as he gazed reflectively at the neatly tended graves of his seven-year-old son Carl and 10-year-old daughter Marylyn.

Minett, whose other daughter Gaynor was one of just 10 little children plucked out alive from a deadly sea of black mud, said: "This is a very sad day for me. For the sake of the other children you have to go on -- but oh, what a price."

Aberfan's Baptist minister Ken Hayes, whose nine-year-old son Dyfrig was among the victims, said before the rows of white Italian marble headstones: "It helps us to come in the early morning and remember those we have lost.
"It is eerie. The weather is like it was that day."
"Let us also remember those with us who are still permanently suffering," he added.
Beside him on the cemetery steps stood Jeff Edwards, who 30 years ago was the last child to be pulled alive from the shattered wreckage of Pantglas school.
A memorial garden now stands on the spot where the children had been singing at the last school assembly before half-term.

Edwards, who now runs a centre for the scores of young jobless in the village, is the first to admit: "You don't want to remember because it brings back so many feelings of guilt and fear. Why was I lucky? Why me?"
In the bitter recriminations that followed the disaster, the official tribunal pinned responsibility on the National Coal Board, the state coal company.
Aberfan's murderous Number Seven tip was found to have been built over a natural spring which soaked and destabilised the colliery waste as if it were on ball-bearings.
Millions of tonnes of slag hurtled down the mountainside at 50 miles an hour (80 kph).
The psychological scars have still not healed for the survivors. Many fear sleeping in the dark. They feel guilty about being spared.
"Here I am, a grown man, tough ex-miner and all that, yet since that day I don't like the dark," said survivor Gerald Kirwan. "Even being at home on my own at night makes me uneasy."
Gaynor Madgwick has helped fellow survivors come to terms with the disaster by writing and publishing a graphic account of the avalanche that killed her brother and sister.

Scribbled in her school exercise book when she was just 12 were the poignant words: "I didn't cry afterwards as I didn't know what was happening. It was all like a dream. Bodies lay crushed and buried.
"As I looked back, I saw my friends dead -- the last time for me to see them."
But it was the tombstones on the 30th anniversary of the disaster that bore the most eloquent tribute to a lost generation.
"And for a little while we had him all to ourselves," read one inscription. "A precious flower lent not given, to bud on earth and bloom in heaven."
